\chapter{Heart}
\label{ch:russian-heart}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the heart in Russian, pronounce its silent letter correctly, and name its cousins across three other languages.}

A one-lesson chapter closing the tranche on \ru{сердце}, the surest cognate in the book: the reader produces the word with its silent \ru{д}, reads the new letter \ru{ц}, names heart, cor and kardía as its cousins, and closes by naming \ru{любить} as the verb the heart does — the last of Chapter 5's atoms to be rescued.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sérdtse]{\ru{сердце} — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} the surest cousin in this book}

\label{lesson:RU-C10-serdtse}



\begin{quote}
One more letter, one silent consonant, and then the tightest Indo-European cognate set this book will show you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{сердце}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{сердце}} — \emph{sérdtse} — \textbf{heart}. \textbf{Neuter.}
\end{quote}

Ends in \textbf{-\ru{це}}, a spelling variant of \textbf{-\ru{о}/-\ru{е}} forced by the letter before it — still Chapter 6's neuter row. Stress on the front: \emph{SYÉRT-se}. And listen closely: the \textbf{\ru{д}} is not pronounced at all. Four consonants in a row would be unsayable, so Russian drops the middle one in speech — write \emph{\ru{сердце}}, say \emph{sérts-e}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Cyrillic.)} One new letter: \textbf{\ru{ц}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{ц}} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}ts,\textquotedblright{}} the sound at the end of English \emph{cat\textbf{s}}. No Latin look-alike to trip over — it simply hasn't been in your way until now.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\ru{с}, \ru{е}, \ru{р}, \ru{д}, \ru{е}} you already have.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{сердце}} is Indo-European *\emph{\'{k}erd-}, and few roots in this book have travelled so far with so little disguise. English \textbf{heart} is the same word. Latin \textbf{cor}, genitive \textbf{cordis}, gave English \textbf{cordial} (\textquotedblleft{}heartfelt\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{courage} (from the heart), and — by a long and surprising road through \textquotedblleft{}to learn by heart\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{record}. Greek \textbf{kardía} gave \textbf{cardiac} and \textbf{cardiology}. Say \emph{sérdtse}, \emph{heart}, \emph{cor}, \emph{kardía} in a row and the family resemblance needs no proof.

It is fitting that the book's most secure cousin is also the organ Chapter 5 gave a verb to: \textbf{\ru{любить}}, with its inserted \textbf{\ru{л}}, is what the \emph{\ru{сердце}} does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сердце}\textquotedblright{} — silent \ru{д}, \emph{SYÉRT-se}
  \item the new letter — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ц} says ts, as in cats\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}heart, cor, kardía\textquotedblright{} — one root, three more languages
  \item all five body words — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ухо}, \ru{нос}, \ru{рот}, \ru{глаз}, \ru{сердце}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{Я} \ru{люблю}\textquotedblright{} — the verb the heart does
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} with its gender, and pronounce it correctly. (\textbf{\ru{Сердце}} — \textbf{neuter} — \emph{sérts-e}, the \textbf{\ru{д}} silent.) What sound does \textbf{\ru{ц}} make? (\textbf{Ts}, as in \emph{cats}.) Name three English words that share its root, beyond \emph{heart} itself. (\textbf{Cordial, courage, record} — from Latin \emph{cor/cordis}; or \textbf{cardiac}, from Greek \emph{kardía}.) Which Chapter 5 verb is what the heart does? (\textbf{\ru{Любить}}, \textquotedblleft{}to love.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
